Query Optimization Basics

Use indexes on columns you filter or join on
Avoid SELECT * — only fetch what you need
Push filters early, before joins
Use EXPLAIN to inspect query plans

-- Before
SELECT * FROM orders JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.id;

-- After
SELECT orders.id, customers.name
FROM orders
JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.id
WHERE orders.status = 'completed';

title: Module 4: Query Optimization
text:
Push Filters Early
-- Slow: joins first, then filters
SELECT * FROM orders
JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.id
WHERE orders.status = 'completed';

-- Fast: filter before join
SELECT o.id, c.name
FROM (SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed') o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id;

title: Species Synonym Search (UBC MDS Capstone Project)
text:
The value of this project to me

Technical skills:

building a full-stack application end-to-end: a Next.js frontend, a FastAPI backend, and a Python data pipeline, all wired together and deployed to cloud platforms (Vercel and Hugging Face Spaces).
designing an extensible API abstraction layer (SpeciesAPI) that allowed 20+ external biodiversity databases to be integrated using a shared contract, making adding new sources a structured, predictable process.
implementing streaming search via Server-Sent Events (SSE) so the UI shows results as they arrive, rather than waiting for all sources to finish.
containerizing the backend with Docker and setting up CI/CD with GitHub Actions.

Collaboration:

working as a team of 4 across the full stack, coordinating ownership of frontend views, backend routes, and individual pipeline source clients.
partnering with an external stakeholder (the museum’s informatics curator) and a faculty mentor, which required translating technical decisions into plain language and aligning the roadmap to real curatorial workflows.

Project management:

scoping and delivering a production-grade system within the capstone timeline, including a test suite with fixture management, API documentation, and a final report.





Overview
The Beaty Biodiversity Museum at UBC maintains millions of specimens organized by current scientific taxonomy. Because taxonomic classifications evolve over time, a single species can carry many different names across publications and databases. Museum curators previously had to check each database manually to reconcile synonyms.
This tool queries 20+ biodiversity databases simultaneously, consolidates the returned names and taxonomic data, and presents curators with five linked views to explore the results. The goal is to surface organized evidence while preserving the curator’s final decision-making authority.
Developed as part of UBC Master of Data Science, DSCI 591 Capstone Program (2025-2026) in partnership with the museum’s informatics team. Team members: Molly Kessler, Wendy Frankel, Johnson Chuang, and myself William Song.


Project repository
GitHub repo: ubc-mds-capstone-project


Live demo

Frontend: ubc-mds-capstone-project.vercel.app
Backend API docs: windforce9e4-species-synonym-api.hf.space/docs




Architecture
The system has three layers:
Browser (Next.js)
      |
FastAPI Backend
      |
Data Pipeline (20+ source clients)

Frontend (frontend/): Next.js (App Router) with React, Mantine v7 components, TanStack Query for data fetching, and Zustand for state. Communicates with the backend over HTTP/JSON.
Backend (backend_api/): FastAPI service exposing search, suggest, sources, and taxonomy endpoints. Live search streams results back via Server-Sent Events at /api/search/stream.
Pipeline (scripts/apis_pipe/): each biodiversity source is a Python class that extends a shared SpeciesAPI abstract base class, implementing five required methods (fetch query data, fetch synonym data, fetch accepted data, compile synonyms, compile accepted name). This contract makes each client independently testable and interchangeable.




Data sources
20+ external biodiversity databases are integrated:

Global backbone: GBIF
Symbiota portals: MyCoPortal, Lichen, Bryophyte, SERNEC, CCH2, NANSH, and others (11 portals total)
Independent APIs: Catalogue of Life, Tropicos, Index Fungorum, GenBank, FishBase, ITIS, Mushroom Observer, Paleobiology Database, MycoBank

Each source returns data normalized to a 16-field standardized schema. The pipeline routes queries to relevant sources based on kingdom (Animalia, Plantae, Fungi), so curators are not shown databases that are irrelevant to the specimen they are researching.



Key features

Five linked views

Overview: every synonym returned, alongside which databases recognize each name.
Relations: interactive graph of synonyms grouped by genus and species, with links to source records.
Timeline: names arranged chronologically by publication year.
Taxonomy: classification across ranks with edit-distance shading to highlight spelling variants versus genuine taxonomic disagreements.
Detail: complete records from all databases with CSV export.



Streaming search
Results stream into the UI via Server-Sent Events as each database responds, so curators see partial results immediately rather than waiting for the slowest source.


Fuzzy name suggestions
When a search returns no results, the app queries GBIF for close matches and presents “Did you mean?” suggestions.




Testing and CI

Unit tests: run offline against recorded API fixture files, no live credentials required. Fixtures are generated by tests/fixtures/regenerate_fixtures.py, which hits real APIs and stores the responses.
Integration tests: marked with @pytest.mark.integration, run against live APIs.
CI: GitHub Actions runs the unit test suite on every pull request.

pytest -m "not integration" tests/   # unit tests (CI mode)
pytest -m integration tests/         # live integration tests



Deployment

Backend: Docker image deployed to a Hugging Face Space (port 7860).
Frontend: Next.js app auto-deployed to Vercel on push to main.
The two layers are connected via the NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL environment variable on the frontend, and CORS is configured on the backend to allow the Vercel domain.




Key takeaways

Abstraction pays off at scale: the SpeciesAPI contract meant adding each new source required touching a predictable set of files rather than scattered ad-hoc code, and kept the test surface manageable across 20+ clients.
Streaming UX changes how users experience latency: showing results as they arrive made the tool feel faster and more transparent than a spinner followed by a full-page result dump.
Working with a real partner sharpens scope decisions: having a curator as the end user (not a classmate) pushed the team to prioritize features that fit actual museum workflows over technically interesting but less useful ones.

title: Smart Amazon Product Query Assistant
text:
Default view of the Amazon Product Search web app



The value of this project to me

Practicing and implementation:

information retrieval methods: BM25, Semantic Search, Hybrid
LLM-based AI Assistant
RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)
real-time product recommendation system

Measurement and evaluation:

designing a 10-query evaluation set across difficulty tiers, then building a reproducible harness that regenerates every comparison table on demand.
quantifying why two retrieval methods disagree instead of asserting it: their top-5 results overlap on only 0.2 of 5 products on average.
running controlled experiments where one variable moves at a time, including a prompt comparison whose result contradicted my prediction.

Data quality investigation:

finding and quantifying three traps in the source data that would each have silently corrupted results, including a metadata field that is wrong for 73% of rows.
writing validation that asserts corpus invariants before a 40-minute indexing step, which caught two real bugs on its first run.

Engineering at scale:

scaling from 94k to 231,568 products, which required streaming ingest, schema-aware caching, and memory profiling.
building staleness guards so a search index can never be silently used against a corpus it was not built from.
138 tests, GitHub Actions CI, and root-causing a segfault from a macOS crash report.

Building LLM systems responsibly:

gating scope on a measured retrieval threshold in code, so off-topic questions are refused before any API call is made.
redacting contact details reviewers volunteered into review text, stripping them in the context builder so the model never receives them.
auditing the corpus for prompt injection, then declining to build the filter it seemed to call for, because all 40 matches were false positives.

Independent follow-through:

taking a graded team project and rebuilding it alone, deliberately, to understand each decision.





Overview
A context-aware product search assistant for Amazon listings. Given a natural language query, it retrieves relevant products and generates an answer grounded in what reviewers actually wrote, showing the exact sources used.
This began as a two-person project for UBC MDS DSCI 575 (Advanced Machine Learning), built with teammate Harrison Li. After the course ended I rebuilt it from scratch, expanding the corpus 2.5x and adding the engineering the original lacked. The goal was to understand every decision well enough to defend it with a measurement.
Almost every figure below is something I measured on the real corpus.


Project repository
GitHub: smart-amazon-product-query-assistant



What I learned, with evidence
Each item links to the full writeup in the repository.

Preprocessing can silently destroy a query before any model sees it
The query quiet dishwasher for a small apartment under $400 returned a 400 CFM range hood. Tracing it:
'quiet dishwasher for a small apartment under $400'
   -> ['quiet', 'dishwasher', 'small', 'apartment', '400']
   dropped: ['for', 'a', 'under']
under is a stopword and $ is not alphanumeric, so BM25 searched for the bare number 400 with no notion of “less than”. The constraint was deleted during tokenization, before ranking began. Semantic search lost the same constraint differently, dissolving it into a 384-dimensional vector where no dimension means “price ceiling”.
The lesson generalized: when a result looks wrong, inspect what the pipeline actually received before suspecting the algorithm.
Full trace through all four retrieval modes


Three data traps, each found by measuring the data








Trap
Measured
Consequence if missed




price is null
50.5% of products
Formatted naively it renders as the string nan, which BM25 then indexes as an ordinary searchable word across half the corpus


main_category is unreliable
only 27.1% of products in the Appliances file are labelled “Appliances”
Category filtering would be wrong for 73% of rows


average_rating is not the review mean
differs by >0.1 for 62,960 of 94,319 products
It is Amazon’s site-wide figure; a document can show “4.4 stars” above reviews averaging 2.88



The nan trap was the subtle one. It survives tokenizer cleaning, because nan looks exactly like a real word, so it had to be fixed at document construction instead.
Dataset reference with all measurements


Two retrieval methods that barely agree, quantified
Across the 10-query evaluation set, BM25 and semantic search shared 0.2 of their top 5 results on average. On most queries the overlap was zero.
That single number is the empirical case for hybrid retrieval: the methods are not better and worse versions of each other, they are complementary. It also reframed several results, because low overlap does not mean one system is wrong. On something two people can play together on the couch the two returned entirely different games and both answer sets were correct.
Per-query retrieval comparison


An experiment whose result contradicted my prediction
I compared three prompt variants on identical retrieved context: a lightly-steered control, one with explicit anti-hallucination rules, and one that constrained only the output shape.
I expected the explicit rules to handle constraints best. The shape-constrained variant was strictest: it alone rejected a $39.99 game as not “under 40 dollars”. Forcing a NOT RECOMMENDED section appears to make the model adjudicate every candidate rather than mention only the easy ones.
Prompt comparison and RAG evaluation


Model scale improves grounding while fluency stays flat
Running an 8B and a 70B model on byte-identical context, both wrote fluent English. The 8B fabricated two prices: it claimed a $370 dishwasher was “above the $400 budget”, and that a $19.99 game was over a $40 budget when the real disqualifier was its platform. Both statements contradicted the context in its own prompt.
The usual RAG failure is a confident wrong fact. That drove two design decisions: the app shows a sources panel so any claim is checkable, and the context builder writes missing values explicitly as price not listed, because a model shown a gap will fill it.
Model comparison on identical context


Scaling the corpus was an engineering problem
Going from 94k to 231,568 products broke naive approaches. What it actually required:

Streaming ingest. DuckDB reads 1.16 GB of gzipped JSONL at roughly 400 MB peak memory; loading it into pandas first would not fit comfortably.
Schema-aware cache invalidation. Checking that a cached file has the right column types as well as the right names. A price column silently written as a string broke numeric filtering while every column name stayed correct.
Corpus fingerprinting. Each index stores categories@n_products#doc_text_sha and refuses to load on a mismatch. The content hash catches an edit to document construction, which leaves the category list and product count identical. It costs 1.5 seconds against the 40 minutes it protects.
Memory profiling. The BM25 index alone occupies 4.1 GB, which turned out to be the constraint that shapes any deployment plan.

Thirteen design decisions with the measurement behind each


Deciding where a guardrail belongs
The app answered “what’s 1+1?”. Retrieval had returned five arbitrary appliances, because top-k retrieval always returns k results however poor the match, so the emptiness check never fired and the model answered from its own knowledge.
The obvious fix is a prompt rule telling the model to decline. That rule takes effect only after the API call is billed, so I put the gate in Python: a threshold on the top-1 cosine, checked before retrieval runs.
Choosing the threshold took a measurement. Off-topic queries scored 0.31 to 0.376; the weakest legitimate query in my evaluation set scored 0.437. A threshold of 0.40 sits between them and classified 11 of 11 queries correctly. The margin is only 0.061, which is the honest caveat: vague-but-real questions and off-topic ones genuinely look alike to an embedding model, so I set the threshold low.
One subtlety made this harder than it looked. The score has to come from the semantic retriever directly, because neither fusion method preserves absolute scale: Reciprocal Rank Fusion emits 1/(60 + rank), so its top score is 1/61 whether a match is perfect or worthless, and weighted fusion min-max normalizes the top result to 1.0 by construction. Gating on a fused score would have let everything through while looking correct. A test now hands the gate a fused score of 1.0 alongside a cosine of 0.30 and asserts refusal, so a future simplification cannot quietly reintroduce the bug.
The same reasoning settled a privacy question. Reviewers had typed their own email addresses and phone numbers into review text: 282 and 112 documents respectively. A prompt rule saying “never repeat contact details” asks the model to hold the data and decline to use it. Stripping it in the context builder means the model never receives it, which is the stronger guarantee.


Knowing which defence not to build
Auditing the same corpus for prompt injection, 40 documents matched instruction-shaped phrases. Reading them, all 40 were ordinary English: “you are now a 4th grader”, “you are now a dryer technician”, and system prompt meaning a shell prompt. Zero were attacks.
That number argues against the defence it seems to invite. A regex filter shipped against this corpus would have run at a 100% false-positive rate, silently degrading 40 legitimate products while catching nothing, and any paraphrase defeats it anyway.
Capability is what bounds injection risk. The model here has no tools, takes no actions, and its output renders as plain text, so the worst an injected review achieves is a bad recommendation. Writing that down changed how I think about agent design generally: the question worth asking is “what can this thing do if the rule fails”.
Prompt injection, and what RAG creates




Dataset

Source: Amazon Reviews 2023 (McAuley Lab, UCSD)
Scale: 231,568 products from 6,753,220 reviews, spanning Appliances (94,319) and Video Games (137,249)
Configurable: any of the dataset’s 34 categories can be selected at build time. Per-category intermediates are cached, so adding one re-downloads only that category.




Architecture
query -> (scope gate) -> retrieve -> build context -> fill prompt -> generate -> answer + sources
Four modes share one interface, so switching is a single argument:







Mode
Method




BM25
Keyword matching with IDF, term-frequency saturation, and length normalization


Semantic
all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings, L2-normalized in a FAISS IndexFlatIP so inner product equals cosine similarity


Hybrid
Reciprocal Rank Fusion, 1/(60 + rank), or weighted score normalization


RAG
Hybrid retrieval, then an LLM reads the reviews and applies constraints retrieval cannot enforce



Because all three retrievers return (parent_asin, score), the RAG pipeline is retriever-agnostic: semantic RAG and hybrid RAG differ by one argument and share the same pipeline.
Models: llama-3.3-70b-versatile (primary) and openai/gpt-oss-20b (comparison), both via Groq, plus a local llama3.1:8b through Ollama for iterating without consuming API quota.
Context is trimmed before it reaches the model. Whole documents produce 4,000 to 6,000 token contexts; title, metadata, and two truncated reviews produce about 600. An 85% reduction with no loss of answer quality, which moved the free-tier budget from roughly 22 to over 80 calls per day.
How RAG works and how the retrievers work, both written as learning notes.



Evaluation
Evaluation runs as a script. python src/evaluate.py regenerates every comparison table, so changing a prompt or a retriever and re-running produces updated results automatically.
One deliberate choice: the qualitative rating columns are left blank by the generator. A model grading its own output is not an evaluation, so the script produces the evidence and I supply the verdicts. Each answer is printed alongside the exact sources the model was given, which makes the check concrete: a product named in an answer but absent from its sources is a fabrication.



Engineering practice

138 tests, running in under 4 seconds with no network and no data files. They target the things that fail silently: tokenization, document construction, corpus invariants, fusion arithmetic, the staleness guards, and the safety gates.
GitHub Actions CI running lint, format check, tests, and a check that every documented CLI still parses. The suite needs no secrets, which is why the workflow stays simple.
Reproducibility treated as a real goal. The pipeline rebuilds from nothing with three commands, and tests pass on a machine with no NLTK corpus downloaded, verified by simulating one.
Ruff for lint and formatting, pinned via pyproject.toml so results do not depend on whichever version happens to be on PATH.




App
A Streamlit app with two tabs. Search returns ranked products with category and price filters. RAG answers a question and displays the answer above the exact sources it was given.

Search tab



Search tab: ranked results for ‘small and cheap ovens’ using hybrid retrieval, with fusion method, category, and price filters




RAG tab
The answer sits above the exact products the model was given. The caption records the retriever, model, prompt, context size, and stage timings, so any answer can be traced back to how it was produced.



RAG tab answering ‘quiet dishwasher for a small apartment under $400’, with the generated answer above a Sources list of the five products supplied to the model


The line under the web-search checkbox reports the gate’s decision before generating, here “will not search (the corpus can answer this without web results)”.
Generation is gated behind an explicit submit button. Streamlit re-runs every tab’s body on every interaction, so an ungated LLM call would fire on any widget change and exhaust the daily API quota within minutes.
An optional web-search tool (Tavily) covers what a fixed 2023 snapshot cannot: current prices and availability. It is gated so it runs only when the question needs it, and results appear in a separate labelled block so web claims stay distinguishable from review evidence.




Installation
git clone https://github.com/canadasung/smart-amazon-product-query-assistant.git
cd smart-amazon-product-query-assistant

conda env create -f environment.yml
conda activate smart-amazon-query-assist

python src/download_data.py     # download, merge, build documents
python src/bm25.py              # keyword index
python src/semantic.py          # FAISS index

streamlit run app/app.py
Retrieval needs no API keys. The RAG features need a Groq key in .env; .env.example documents every variable.



Key takeaways

Measure before asserting. Nearly every design decision here is defensible because a number backs it: the 0.2/5 retrieval overlap, the 50.5% null prices, the 85% context reduction, the 4.1 GB index. Each one changed what I built.
The most expensive bugs are the silent ones. A nan in half the corpus, a price column typed as a string, a stale index serving confident wrong answers. None of them raised an error. That is why the project has validation, staleness guards, and tests aimed at exactly those paths.
Be willing to be wrong in public. The prompt experiment contradicted my prediction, and saying so made the writeup more useful.
Verification has to match the failure mode. Checking that a server returns HTTP 200 does not prove a query works. I learned that from a segfault my own testing had missed.
Put the guarantee where it cannot be argued with. Leaving data out of the context is stronger than asking a model not to repeat it. The same reasoning moved scope checking into a threshold in code, where it also stops costing API quota.

title: World Education Project
text:
The value of this group project to me

Technical skills:

deploying a Shiny dashboard to share insights interactively on Posit Cloud, a great substitute if Tableau or Power BI are not available.
applying data cleaning, EDA, visualization, and dashboarding techniques.

Collaboration:

working with a team of 4 data science students to divide tasks, share insights, and integrate work into a cohesive project.

Project management:

coordinating timelines, version control, and communication to ensure smooth progress.





Overview
This project analyzes global education indicators to explore patterns in enrollment, attainment, and inequality across countries. The analysis was completed as part of UBC Master of Data Science, DSCI 532 Data Visualization course and demonstrates data cleaning, exploratory analysis, visualization, and basic modeling to surface insights relevant to education gaps between genders and international regions. Then finally, deploy the insights in an interactive dashboard built with Shiny, and a chatbot interface using a large language model to query the data.


Project repository
Forked project repo: World Education Project (mirrored from school repo because it is not publicly accessible)



Data
Primary files (from the repo)

data/processed/processed_global_education.csv: cleaned, merged dataset used for analysis.

data/raw/Global_Education.csv: raw source files sourced from Kaggle - World Educational Data, compiled from UNESCO Institute for Statistics, UNICEF, and UN Statistics Division.

title: Market Basket Analysis
text:
The value of this project to me

Business analytics skills:

applying affinity analysis (Market Basket Analysis) to uncover product co-occurrence patterns from transactional data.
translating data mining concepts (Support, Confidence, Lift) into a practical, business-friendly cross-selling tool.

Communication:

presenting a technical analytics method to business stakeholders using a worked example (bread & butter) and clear SMART criteria.


Presentation Slides



Overview
Market Basket Analysis (MBA) — also known as affinity analysis — is a data mining technique based on conditional probability (Bayes’ Theorem) used to discover co-occurrence relationships among products (the classic “beers and diapers” example). It is widely adopted across retail, e-commerce, and finance for cross-sell/upsell strategy, bundling and discounting, shelf or page placement, and fraud detection.



Why Market Basket Analysis

Easy to understand and implement: gather transactional data with a defined “basket” (e.g., by customer or by transaction).
Widely applicable: cross-sell/upsell, bundle/discount strategy, shelf or webpage display optimization, and fraud pattern detection in finance.




Analytic Terms

Occurrence & Support
Occurrence / Co-occurrence: the number of times an item (or set of items) is purchased within the group.
Support: the frequency (ratio) of an occurrence within the group.
Worked example — out of 100 customers:

Bread is purchased by 50 customers → Support(Bread) = 50/100 = 0.5
Butter is purchased by 30 customers → Support(Butter) = 30/100 = 0.3
Bread and Butter together are purchased 20 times → Support(Co-occurrence) = 20/100 = 0.2



Confidence
Confidence: the probability of both items being purchased, given that one item was purchased.
\[
Confidence(Bread) = \frac{Support(Co\text{-}occur)}{Support(Bread)} = \frac{0.2}{0.5} = 0.4
\]
\[
Confidence(Butter) = \frac{Support(Co\text{-}occur)}{Support(Butter)} = \frac{0.2}{0.3} = 0.6667
\]


Lift
Lift: the key indicator — the likelihood that two products go together. Only meaningful when greater than 1 (the higher, the stronger the association), though there is no universal market standard for “high enough”; values are interpreted relative to other outputs.
\[
Lift(Bread \,\&\, Butter) = \frac{Support(Co\text{-}occur)}{Support(Bread) \times Support(Butter)} = \frac{0.2}{0.15} = 1.33
\]




Benefits of MBA

Accurate and easy to read: Support, Confidence, and Lift are simple, interpretable metrics.
Automation is possible: all products analyzed in under 10 minutes, versus manual correlation analysis comparing only 3–4 products per day.
Balances data cleanliness vs. time cost: different levels of data cleanliness still reveal similar patterns.
Additional insights: product popularity, and comparisons across years, seasons, or stores.




Constraints

Similar product formats are still compared: e.g., 1L milk vs. 2L milk. Mitigate by using filtering features to screen products.
Basic MBA is limited to 1-to-1 relationships: e.g., product A and product B. Advanced MBA (A + B + C → D) requires more advanced software/services.
Data cleaning and model maintenance:

Data training is required.
Raw data needs cleaning to reduce model run time.
Procedures must be modified or re-created if the analysis goals change (e.g., changes to the basket or product hierarchy).





Conclusion — SMART in Creating MBA Analytics

Specific: can be measured under different product hierarchies.
Measurable: Support, Confidence, and Lift indicators support decision-making.
Achievable: cost-effective when there’s no budget for external software licenses for the functionality and require self-build.
Relevant: directly matches cross-selling strategy goals.
Timeliness: automation enables fast, easy-to-learn results.

title: Washrooms in Vancouver Parks
text:
The value of this group project to me

Technical skills:

creating a containerized environment using Docker to practice a reproducible workflow.
applying data cleaning, EDA, machine learning models (baseline, KNN, SVM RBF), and visualization techniques.

Collaboration:

working with a team of 3 data science students to divide tasks, share insights, and integrate work into a cohesive project.

Project management:

coordinating timelines, version control, and communication to ensure smooth progress.





Overview
This project maps and analyzes public washroom availability in Vancouver parks. It combines spatial data, park metadata, and accessibility attributes to identify coverage gaps and inform planning decisions for park amenities. The analysis was completed as part of UBC Master of Data Science, DSCI 522 Data Science Workflow course.


Project repository
GitHub repo: washrooms-in-vancouver-parks



Report
The final report can be found here: Predicting the Presence of Washrooms in Vancouver Parks.



Data

Source and scope

City of Vancouver Parks dataset (Vancouver 2025) covering 218 parks with facility attributes, locations, and sizes.



Key variables used

Target: washrooms (presence/absence).
Predictors: park size (hectares), neighbourhood, official park flag, advisories, counts of additional facilities, and special features.



Notes and limitations

The dataset is cross‑sectional and may omit contextual features (visitor counts, funding cycles) that could improve predictive performance.





Methods & Analytics

Exploratory analysis

Compare distributions of binary amenities and park size between parks with and without washrooms (frequency plots, histograms).



Modeling approach

Baseline: Dummy classifier to set a reference accuracy.
Models tested: K‑Nearest Neighbors (KNN) and Support Vector Machine with RBF kernel (SVM RBF).
Validation: 70/30 train/test split with 5‑fold cross‑validation on training data.
Preprocessing: Standardize numeric features; encode categorical predictors (neighbourhood, flags); handle missingness prior to fitting.



Evaluation metrics

Cross‑validation test score, training score, and confusion matrix on held‑out test set to assess generalization and class balance.





Key Findings

Parks with washrooms tend to be larger: median hectare is higher for parks that include washrooms.
Washroom presence correlates with other amenities: parks offering more facilities are more likely to have washrooms.
SVM RBF outperformed KNN and the baseline: in cross‑validation, though the improvement over the dummy baseline was modest, indicating limited predictive signal in the chosen features.
KNN showed signs of overfitting: (higher training score, lower test performance) and therefore generalized poorly.
Implication: richer features (e.g., visitor counts, park usage, funding/prioritization data) or alternative modeling strategies are likely needed to produce stronger, actionable predictions.

title: Model Interpretation
text:
The value of this group project to me

Technical skills:

creating reusable functions and scripts for data preprocessing, modeling, and evaluation to promote reproducibility and scalability.
exploring new platform Netlify for hosting and sharing data science projects.
applying data cleaning, EDA, machine learning models (baseline, KNN, SVM RBF), and visualization techniques.

Collaboration:

working with a team of 3 data science students to divide tasks, share insights, and integrate work into a cohesive project.

Project management:

coordinating timelines, version control, and communication to ensure smooth progress.
pushing code to GitHub and deploying the final report on Netlify for public access.





Overview
model_auto_interpret is a Python package that streamlines the repetitive parts of building and comparing scikit-learn classification models — hyperparameter tuning, cross-model comparison, and performance evaluation. Rather than rewriting the same boilerplate for every project, the package wraps these steps into three reusable functions, sitting in the gap between scikit-learn’s low-level utilities and visualization-only libraries like mlxtend. The package was built as part of UBC Master of Data Science, DSCI 524 Collaborative Software Development course, with a team of 3: Daisy (Ying) Zhou, Yasaman Baher, and myself.


Project repository
GitHub repo: ml-model_interpretation (mirrored from school repo because it is not publicly accessible)


Documentation & tutorial
Docs site: machine-learning-model-interpretation.netlify.app — deployed on Netlify, including a full tutorial and API reference.



Installation
pip install -i https://test.pypi.org/simple/ model-auto-interpret



Key Functions
The package centers on three functions covering the typical model-development workflow:

param_tuning_summary: takes a fitted GridSearchCV/RandomizedSearchCV object and returns a clean summary dataframe of the best parameters and scores, plus the best estimator ready to use.
model_cv_metric_compare: evaluates multiple unfitted models side-by-side via cross-validation, returning accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and ROC-AUC in a single comparison table.
model_evaluation_plotting: scores a fitted model on held-out test data, returning accuracy/F2 metrics, a confusion matrix table, and a ready-to-plot confusion matrix display.




Tutorial walkthrough
The package tutorial demonstrates the full workflow on the Breast Cancer dataset (455 training samples, 30 features, binary classification):

Compare models: model_cv_metric_compare() runs 5-fold cross-validation across Logistic Regression, SVC variants, Random Forest, Decision Tree, and Gradient Boosting, producing a single comparison table.
Tune hyperparameters: param_tuning_summary() extracts the best parameter configuration from GridSearchCV/RandomizedSearchCV results for the top candidate models.
Evaluate on test data: model_evaluation_plotting() scores the tuned model on the test set and generates a confusion matrix visualization.

Result: Random Forest emerged as the top performer at ~96% cross-validation accuracy. The tutorial closes with an end-to-end example on the Iris dataset, reaching 100% test accuracy.



Key takeaways

Less boilerplate, more reproducibility: collapsing tuning, comparison, and evaluation into three function calls makes model-development notebooks shorter and easier for teammates to rerun.
Designed for collaboration: built with packaging best practices (tests, CI, semantic versioning, hosted docs) as the core learning objective of the course, not just the modeling logic itself.

title: Calculating Customer Lifetime Value
text:
The value of this project to me

Business analytics skills:

translating a core marketing/finance metric (CLV) into approachable formulas and examples for a non-technical audience.
comparing historical vs. predictive methods and understanding the trade-offs between simplicity, accuracy, and cost.

Communication:

structuring a technical topic into a 19-slide presentation with worked examples, suitable for stakeholders without a statistics background.


Presentation Slides



Overview
Customer Lifetime Value (CLV), also commonly known as LTV, estimates the total net profit a business can expect from a customer over the duration of their relationship. This presentation covers why CLV matters, the major families of CLV calculation methods, and worked examples for each.


Definition of a Cohort
Groups customers by acquisition period or channel (e.g., signup month or marketing channel) and tracks their cumulative revenue over time. The way of grouping can vary based on the business context and the insights sought.


Why CLV is hard
There is no single “correct” way to calculate CLV — every method involves assumptions and trade-offs.

Even well-built models typically carry 15–25% error margins.
CLV is usually applied to 3–7 year forecasting horizons, so small errors compound.
Every approach faces the same dilemma: a CLV model construction can be at most two of Simple, Accurate, and Inexpensive — never all three.




Historical CLV
Historical methods look backward at actual customer revenue/profit data.

ARPU / ARPA method
Average Revenue Per User (ARPU) or Average Revenue Per Account (ARPA) multiplies average revenue per customer by the expected customer lifespan.
Worked example — Alice vs. Bob
Alice: (150 + 50 + 100) / 6 months = $50 ARPU, 6 months lifespan → CLV = $300
Bob: (45 + 75 +100) / 2 months = $110 ARPU, 2 months lifespan → CLV = $220
(50 + 110) / 2 = $80 per customer
12 months value: $80 * 12 months = $960
24 months value: $80 * 24 months = $1,920

Alice spends less per month but stays subscribed much longer than Bob.
Even though Bob’s monthly spend is higher, Alice’s longer retention can make her CLV greater — illustrating why retention matters as much as spend.



Key points of Historical CLV methods
There are some factors that may not be captured by historical methods:

Different customers have different behavior patterns that may not be reflected in averages. Use cohort method to narrow down to more specific segments.
Future changes in customer behavior or market conditions may not be captured, such as internally changed by offerings or externally changed by market trends.
Not enough data when a business is too young or data duration is too short to capture the full customer lifecycle.





Predictive CLV
Predictive methods use statistical models to forecast future value rather than relying solely on historical averages.

Key Variables
Four variables drive most predictive CLV calculations:

Acquisition Cost / Retention Cost:

The cost to acquire a new customer or retain an existing one (e.g., marketing spend per conversion).

Net Profit Margin:

Among the cohorts, the share of revenue retained as profit after costs.
Profit Margin Ratio: Net Income / Net Sales
Usually the Finance team can provide this number, but if not, general rules are:

10% for public companies
15% for private companies that are scaling predictably
20%-25% for private companies that have not yet reached scale and predictable growth


Retention / Churn Rate and Expected Lifespan:

\[
\text{Retention Rate} = \frac{\text{Customers at End of Period} - \text{New Customers Acquired}}{\text{Customers at Start of Period}}
\]
The Churn Rate is the complement of the Retention Rate: \[
\text{Churn Rate} = 1 - \text{Retention Rate}
\]
We can use the retention rate to estimate the expected customer lifespan: \[
\text{Expected Customer Lifespan} = \frac{1}{\text{Churn Rate}}
\]

Discount Rate:

Accounts for the time value of money when projecting future profits to present value. Get this from the Finance team, or use 1 as a starting point for simplicity.



Formula
After getting the key variables, we can plug them into the formula to calculate CLV:

Simple formula
\[
CLV = \text{Average Revenue per Customer} \times \text{Expected Customer Lifespan}
\]


Complete formula
A more complete formula incorporates profit margins, retention, and the time value of money:
\[
CLV = \left( \frac{\text{Revenue per Customer} \times \text{Gross Margin}}{1 - \text{Retention Rate} + \text{Discount Rate}} \right) - \text{Acquisition Cost}
\]




Conclusion
CLV ultimately helps answer three fundamental business questions:

How much should we spend to acquire a customer?
Which customer segments are worth investing in retaining?
How sustainable is our current growth strategy?

Choosing a CLV method is less about finding the “perfect” formula and more about matching the right balance of simplicity, accuracy, and cost to the decision at hand.



References

For Entrepreneurs — What’s your TRUE customer lifetime value (LTV)?
Kaushik.net — Excellent Analytics Tip #17: Calculate Customer Lifetime Value
Above the Crowd — The Dangerous Seduction of the Lifetime Value (LTV) Formula
Wikipedia — Customer Lifetime Value

title: Species name search
text: This project builds a production-grade species name search tool that aggregates results from over 15 external biodiversity databases including GBIF and Symbiota portals.

title: Species name search
text:
Problem
Biodiversity researchers often need to reconcile species names across multiple taxonomic authorities. No single API covers all databases, and sequential requests are too slow for interactive use.

title: Species name search
text:
Approach

Async fan-out: Used httpx with asyncio.gather to query all APIs concurrently, reducing median latency from ~8s sequential to ~1.2s.
Redis caching: Common species names are cached with a 24-hour TTL, cutting repeat query cost to near zero.
PostgreSQL: Stores canonical name mappings and user search history.
Next.js frontend: Displays ranked results with source attribution and fuzzy match scores.

title: Species name search
text:
Key code
import asyncio
import httpx

async def fan_out(name: str, sources: list[str]) -> dict:
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=5.0) as client:
        tasks = [query_source(client, name, src) for src in sources]
        results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks, return_exceptions=True)
    return {src: r for src, r in zip(sources, results) if not isinstance(r, Exception)}

title: When to use DuckDB vs pandas for local analytics
text: Both DuckDB and pandas can handle local analytical workloads, but they have very different performance profiles. After hitting pandas memory limits on a 5M-row CSV, I did a side-by-side comparison.

title: When to use DuckDB vs pandas for local analytics
text:
The short answer
Use DuckDB when:

Your dataset is larger than ~500MB
You are doing aggregations, joins, or window functions
You want to query Parquet or CSV files without loading them into memory

Use pandas when:

You need row-wise Python logic (.apply, custom functions)
You are doing iterative data cleaning with lots of intermediate steps
The dataset fits comfortably in memory and transformation is simple

title: When to use DuckDB vs pandas for local analytics
text:
Benchmark
import duckdb
import pandas as pd
import time

# DuckDB aggregation
start = time.perf_counter()
duckdb.sql("SELECT category, AVG(value) FROM 'data.parquet' GROUP BY category").df()
print(f"DuckDB: {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f}s")

# pandas equivalent
start = time.perf_counter()
df = pd.read_parquet("data.parquet")
df.groupby("category")["value"].mean()
print(f"pandas: {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f}s")
On 5M rows: DuckDB finished in 0.3s, pandas in 2.1s – and pandas used 1.4GB RAM vs DuckDB’s 180MB.

title: When to use DuckDB vs pandas for local analytics
text:
Takeaway
DuckDB is not a replacement for pandas. They compose well: use DuckDB to filter and aggregate down to a manageable size, then hand off to pandas for Python-native transformations.
